Use [`dim()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/16_Piping/Piping.html#/two-types-of-pipes-you-might-see) to print the number of rows and columns. The number of rows should match what you got at the end of Lab 2. ::: callout-note #### Projects 1 and 3: you will still see missing data, and that's okay! Some variables in `wbns_04_no_na` are still very missing on purpose. They are missing because of skip logic (people who were never asked the question because an earlier answer already told us), and we didn't drop them in Lab 2. - **Project 1:** `Q25A` and `Q26A` are only asked of people who said no to `Q25` or `Q26`. You don't need them for your composite score. Leave them as they are, and don't drop rows because of them. - **Project 3:** `medicaid_chip_q53`, `housing_q53`, `housing_q11`, and `benefit_wic`. You'll handle these when you build `total_benefits`. You'll see this missing data again in your quick summaries. Note it, but don't remove it. ::: ::: callout-important #### Task From the `.rda` file you exported at the end of Lab 2, import `wbns_04_no_na` into R using `import()` from the `rio` package. Save it as an object called `wbns_04_no_na`. Use `dim()` to print the number of rows and columns to verify the import. ::: ### Clean up extra white space **White space** is any character you can't see: spaces, tabs, and line breaks. Sometimes survey data comes with an extra space at the end of a category, so the answer is stored as `"Yes "` instead of `"Yes"`. You can't see the difference when R prints the data, but **R treats them as two different values**. That means `benefit_snap == "Yes"` would be `FALSE` for every `"Yes "`, and your composite score would quietly turn into `NA`. (This is the same idea as the "spelling/spacing is important" slides in Lesson 23.) Some of the WBNS variables have extra spaces like this, especially in Project 3. We'll remove them from **every** factor before building the composite score. It's a good habit even if your project doesn't have the problem. The function that removes extra white space is [`trimws()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/trimws.html) (**trim** **w**hite **s**pace). It removes spaces from the beginning and end of text, but leaves the spaces between words alone: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trimws("Yes ") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Yes" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} trimws(" Don't know ") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Don't know" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} trimws("Some of the time") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Some of the time" ``` ::: ::: 1. **Look for extra spaces.** Use [`levels()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/23_Data_transformation_advanced/Data_transformation_advanced.html#/i-can-make-degree-a-factor-variable) (Lesson 23) on one of your main variables to see its categories in quotes. In quotes, a trailing space is visible: `"Yes "` instead of `"Yes"`. Use the variable from your project's tab below. 2. **Remove extra spaces from every factor.** This code uses the same pattern as the code you used in Lab 1 to remove the numbers in parentheses from the categories. Instead of `gsub()`, it uses `trimws()`. Copy it into your editing file as is: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_04_trimmed <- wbns_04_no_na |> mutate( across( where(is.factor), ~ { levels(.) <- trimws(levels(.)) . } ) ) ``` ::: `across(where(is.factor), ...)` means "do this to every factor variable," and `levels(.) <- trimws(levels(.))` replaces each factor's categories with their trimmed versions. If a variable had both `"Yes"` and `"Yes "` as categories, they are now combined into one `"Yes"`. 3. **Check your work.** Run `levels()` on the same variable again, using `wbns_04_trimmed`. The extra spaces should be gone. Then use [`dim()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/16_Piping/Piping.html#/two-types-of-pipes-you-might-see) to confirm the number of rows and columns didn't change. ::: {.panel-tabset group="project"} #### Project 1 Check `levels(wbns_04_no_na$ease_find_place)` before and `levels(wbns_04_trimmed$ease_find_place)` after. #### Project 2 Check `levels(wbns_04_no_na$trust_provider)` before and `levels(wbns_04_trimmed$trust_provider)` after. #### Project 3 Check `levels(wbns_04_no_na$mh_nervous)` before and `levels(wbns_04_trimmed$mh_nervous)` after. The mental health items are where the extra spaces are: look closely at the quotes in the "before" output, and you'll see categories like `"Most of the time "`. Without trimming, `mh_nervous == "Most of the time"` would never be `TRUE`. ::: ::: callout-tip #### Did Lab 2 miss anything because of extra spaces? If a category like `"Don't know "` had a trailing space, then `replace_with_na()` in Lab 2 may not have matched it. That's okay: those values are still categories (not `NA`) in your data. When you build your composite score, they won't match any line in your [`case_when()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/23_Data_transformation_advanced/Data_transformation_advanced.html#/what-does-case_when-do), so they'll become `NA` there, and the `NA` checks in the next section will catch them. ::: ::: callout-important #### Task Use `trimws()` to remove extra white space from the categories of every factor variable. Save the result as `wbns_04_trimmed`. Use `levels()` on one of your main variables before and after to show the extra spaces are gone, and use `dim()` to confirm no rows or columns were lost. ::: ### Construct the composite score ::: callout-caution Please make sure you are referencing the PDF with the questionnaire when creating your composite score. There are important descriptions and caveats in the questionnaire! ::: Your project must create a brand-new variable that combines information from at least two source columns using [`mutate()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/mutate-transform-and-create-variables). Start from `wbns_04_trimmed`. The table at the top of this lab lists the variables to combine, and your project's tab below walks you through it. **The general recipe** (the same for every project): 1. **Confirm the response scale** for each item in the questionnaire. Is it Yes/No? A 5-point scale? What order are the levels in? 2. **Convert each item to a number** using [`case_when()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/23_Data_transformation_advanced/Data_transformation_advanced.html#/what-does-case_when-do) inside `mutate()` (Lesson 23). Write one line for each category: `item == "Category" ~ number`. Save each converted item as a **new** variable ending in `_num` (e.g., `ease_find_place_num`), so you can compare it to the original. - Any value that doesn't match one of your conditions (including `NA`) automatically becomes `NA`. That's what we want! 3. **Check each conversion** with [`tabyl()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/28_Data_summarization_tables/Data_summarization_tables.html#/what-does-tabyl-do), using the pattern from Lesson 25: `wbns_05_composite |> tabyl(ease_find_place, ease_find_place_num)`. Every category should line up with the number you intended. 4. **Add the converted items together** into one new composite variable inside `mutate()`, using the required name from your project's tab. 5. **Sanity-check the result:** use [`summary()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/27_Data_summarization_quick/Data_summarization_quick.html#/what-does-summary-do) on your composite score, and confirm the minimum and maximum are within the possible range. Does a higher score mean *more* of what you think it means? - **Check for `NA`s.** You removed missing values in Lab 2, so `ease_free_food`, `trust_courtesy_respect`, and `mental_health_score` should have **no** `NA`s. If `summary()` shows an `NA's` count, some category didn't match any line in your `case_when()`. Usually that's a "Refused" or "Don't know" that wasn't turned into `NA` in Lab 2 Part A, or a spelling mismatch. Use `tabyl()` on the original item and its `_num` version to find it. (Project 3's `total_benefits` can have a few `NA`s; step 5 in your tab handles those.) ::: callout-warning #### Why not `as.numeric()`? You might see code online that converts survey answers with `as.numeric()`. **Don't use it for this lab.** Our variables are factors, and `as.numeric()` gives each level's *position* in the list of levels, **not** the survey's number for that answer. If a factor's first level is `"Refused"`, then `"Very difficult"` becomes 2 instead of 1, and your whole score shifts without any error message. `case_when()` lets you say exactly which number goes with which answer. ::: To keep it easy to debug, build your composite in **two steps**: - **Step A:** one `mutate()` that creates all of your `_num` variables (your tab has the code to start from). Check them with `tabyl()` before moving on. - **Step B:** a second `mutate()` that adds them together. You can add on to the same object, like this (Project 1 shown): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_05_composite <- wbns_05_composite |> mutate( ease_free_food = ease_find_place_num + ease_transport_num + ease_variety_num + ease_timely_num ) ``` ::: Starting a pipeline with the same object you're saving to (`wbns_05_composite <- wbns_05_composite |> ...`) updates that object with your new variable. ::: {.panel-tabset group="project"} #### Project 1 **Composite name:** `ease_free_food` Your composite combines the four `ease_` items, which each ask how difficult or easy a different aspect of accessing free groceries/meals was (finding a place, finding transportation, variety of food, and getting there in a reasonable time). Per the questionnaire, the response scale is **Very difficult (1), Difficult (2), Neither difficult nor easy (3), Easy (4), Very easy (5), Don't know (6)**. 1. You already turned `"Don't know"` into `NA` in Lab 2, so you only need to convert five categories. 2. Convert each item with `case_when()`. Here is the first one; write the other three the same way: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_05_composite <- wbns_04_trimmed |> mutate( ease_find_place_num = case_when( ease_find_place == "Very difficult" ~ 1, ease_find_place == "Difficult" ~ 2, ease_find_place == "Neither difficult nor easy" ~ 3, ease_find_place == "Easy" ~ 4, ease_find_place == "Very easy" ~ 5 ) # add ease_transport_num, ease_variety_num, and ease_timely_num here ) ``` ::: Check that the category spelling matches your `tabyl()` output exactly. 3. Higher values already mean *easier*, so no reverse-coding is needed. 4. Add the four `_num` items together into `ease_free_food`. 5. With 4 items on a 1-5 scale, the possible range is 4 (very difficult across the board) to 20 (very easy across the board). Check that your `summary()` falls in this range. #### Project 2 **Composite name:** `trust_courtesy_respect` Your composite combines `courtesy_respect` (Q108B_1: "I am treated with courtesy and respect by my personal health care provider") and `trust_provider` (Q108B_2: "I trust my personal health care provider"). Per the questionnaire, both share the same response scale: **Never true (1), Rarely true (2), Sometimes true (3), Often true (4), Always true (5)**. 1. Convert each item with `case_when()`. Here is the first one; write the second the same way: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_05_composite <- wbns_04_trimmed |> mutate( courtesy_respect_num = case_when( courtesy_respect == "Never true" ~ 1, courtesy_respect == "Rarely true" ~ 2, courtesy_respect == "Sometimes true" ~ 3, courtesy_respect == "Often true" ~ 4, courtesy_respect == "Always true" ~ 5 ) # add trust_provider_num here ) ``` ::: Check that the category spelling matches your `tabyl()` output exactly. 2. Higher values already mean *more* trust/courtesy/respect, so no reverse-coding is needed. 3. Add the two `_num` items together into `trust_courtesy_respect`. It will range from 2 (never true on both) to 10 (always true on both). Check that your `summary()` falls in this range. 4. *Optional:* if you kept `Q70F_4` and `Q70F_5`, you could build a second, related composite capturing whether the respondent felt judged unfairly based on gender identity or sexual orientation, and compare it against your trust/courtesy/respect score. #### Project 3 **Composite names:** `mental_health_score` and `total_benefits` This project asks for *two* composite scores, and both have a wrinkle worth slowing down for. Don't try to do it all in one `mutate()`. Build it up piece by piece. **Mental health composite** (`mental_health_score`, from the six `mh_` items): These six items ask how often in the past 30 days the respondent felt nervous, hopeless, restless/fidgety, so sad that nothing could cheer them up, that everything was an effort, or worthless. Per the questionnaire, the scale is **All of the time (1), Most of the time (2), Some of the time (3), A little of the time (4), None of the time (5)**. That means a *lower* number = more frequent distress (worse mental health), and a *higher* number = less frequent distress (better mental health). 1. Decide which direction you want your composite to run, and say so in your write-up: - **Option A:** Use the survey's numbers as-is (`"All of the time" ~ 1`, ..., `"None of the time" ~ 5`). Your total will run low = worse, high = better. - **Option B:** Flip the numbers in your `case_when()` (`"All of the time" ~ 5`, ..., `"None of the time" ~ 1`). Your total will run low = better, high = worse, which many people find more intuitive. 2. Convert all six items with `case_when()`, using the same direction for every item. Here is the first one, using Option A: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_05_composite <- wbns_04_trimmed |> mutate( mh_nervous_num = case_when( mh_nervous == "All of the time" ~ 1, mh_nervous == "Most of the time" ~ 2, mh_nervous == "Some of the time" ~ 3, mh_nervous == "A little of the time" ~ 4, mh_nervous == "None of the time" ~ 5 ) # add the other five mh_ items here ) ``` ::: 3. Add the six `_num` items together into `mental_health_score`. The possible range is 6 to 30. **Total benefits composite** (`total_benefits`) — this is the tricky part: The `Q53_` series asks about several *different* benefit programs, each a separate Yes/No question, not a scale. Two of them have **built-in skip logic** (which you saw in your `gg_miss_fct()` plots in Lab 2): - `medicaid_chip_q53` (Q53_B) is *only asked* of people who did **not** already report Medicaid/CHIP coverage in Q31 (item d). If someone said `"Covered"` on `medicaid_chip_q31`, they were skipped past Q53_B, so it is missing for them, even though they clearly do have this benefit. People who said "Not Covered" or "Not Sure" on Q31 **were** asked Q53_B. - `housing_q53` (Q53_C) has the same issue with `housing_q11` ("is your household paying lower rent because a government program is paying part of the cost?"). Anyone who said `"Yes"` on Q11 was skipped past Q53_C. Everyone else was asked Q53_C, including homeowners who never saw Q11. Here's how the two questions in each pair fit together: | What they said on Q31 item d (or Q11) | Asked Q53_B (or Q53_C)? | Receives the benefit? | |---|---|---| | "Covered" (or "Yes") | No, skipped | **Yes** (1) | | Anything else, or not asked | Yes | Use their Q53 answer: "Yes" = 1, "No" = 0 | | Anything else, and Q53 is `NA` (e.g., "Don't know") | Yes | Unknown (`NA`) | 1. **Combine each skipped pair into one 0/1 indicator.** Count the person as receiving the benefit (1) if *either* question says yes. Count them as not receiving it (0) only if they were asked Q53 and said `"No"`. Here is Medicaid/CHIP: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} medicaid_chip = case_when( medicaid_chip_q53 == "Yes" | medicaid_chip_q31 == "Covered" ~ 1, medicaid_chip_q53 == "No" ~ 0 ) ``` ::: If both questions are missing, neither condition is true, so `medicaid_chip` becomes `NA`. Write `housing` the same way, using `housing_q53` and `housing_q11`. 2. **Convert the other benefit items** to 0/1 indicators with `case_when()` (`"Yes" ~ 1`, `"No" ~ 0`). Name each one with `_num` at the end (e.g., `benefit_snap_num`). - `benefit_school_meals` is only asked of households with a child aged 5-18. Your population filter already requires that, so everyone in your sample should have an answer. - `benefit_wic` is only asked of households with a child aged 0-5, which your population filter does **not** guarantee. WIC may be missing for many people because they weren't asked, not because they refused. Decide whether to include WIC in your total at all. If you do, use [`replace_na()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/25_Missing_data_transformations/Missing_data_transformations.html#/replace_na-replace-missing-values-with-a-specific-value) from Lesson 25 to fill in missing `benefit_wic_num` values with 0 instead of dropping those rows, and explain your choice. (Because you turned "Don't know" into `NA` in Lab 2, this also counts the few people who answered "Don't know" about WIC as not receiving it. Mention that in your explanation.) 3. **Check** each indicator with `tabyl()`. For the combined pairs, check against both originals, e.g. `wbns_05_composite |> tabyl(medicaid_chip_q53, medicaid_chip_q31)` next to `wbns_05_composite |> tabyl(medicaid_chip)`. 4. **Add every 0/1 indicator together** into `total_benefits`, a count of how many *different* types of benefits the household receives. 5. **Remove rows with an unknown score.** If any indicator is `NA` (for example, someone who said "Don't know" on Q53_B and wasn't covered on Q31), `total_benefits` will be `NA`, because `1 + NA` is `NA`. The same goes for `mental_health_score` if one of the `mh_` items is `NA` (for example, a "Refused" that wasn't turned into `NA` in Lab 2). Use [`dim()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/16_Piping/Piping.html#/two-types-of-pipes-you-might-see), then remove those rows, then use `dim()` again: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(wbns_05_composite) wbns_05_composite <- wbns_05_composite |> drop_na(total_benefits, mental_health_score) dim(wbns_05_composite) ``` ::: This should remove only a small number of rows. If it removes a lot, check your `_num` variables with `tabyl()`: a category that didn't match any line in your `case_when()` (like an untrimmed `"Yes "`) is the usual cause. ::: ::: callout-important #### Task Create your new composite score(s) using `case_when()` and `mutate()`, following the steps for your project. Where do most composite scores fall? ::: ### Create categories for your composite score(s) A composite score is precise, but it's hard to explain at a glance: "the average score was 14.3" means less to a general audience than "most people reported easy access." In this section, you'll create a **categorical version** of each composite score, so you have both versions for Lab 4 and your final project. We'll use [`case_when()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/23_Data_transformation_advanced/Data_transformation_advanced.html#/what-does-case_when-do) again, this time with ranges of numbers instead of categories. This is the same idea as the income example in Lesson 23 (`income < 30000 ~ "<$30,000"`). 1. **Choose your cut points.** Start with the suggested categories in your project's tab. Use your quick summaries to check that each category will have a reasonable number of people in it. If one category would be nearly empty, it's okay to adjust the cut points or combine two categories. Just explain why. 2. **Create the categories** with `case_when()` inside [`mutate()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/22_Data_transformation_columns/Data_transformation_columns.html#/mutate-transform-and-create-variables). Write one line per category, using `>=` and `<=` with `&` to give each range. Use the **exact** new variable name from your tab (it ends in `_cat`). For example, for Project 1: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_06_cat <- wbns_05_composite |> mutate( ease_free_food_cat = case_when( ease_free_food >= 4 & ease_free_food <= 9 ~ "Difficult access", ease_free_food >= 10 & ease_free_food <= 15 ~ "Moderate access", ease_free_food >= 16 & ease_free_food <= 20 ~ "Easy access" ) ) ``` ::: Make sure every possible score fits into exactly one range, with no gaps (for example, 9 and 10 are in different categories, and nothing falls between them). 3. **Put the categories in order.** `case_when()` gives you text, and R will sort text alphabetically ("Difficult", "Easy", "Moderate"). That would put your categories out of order in every table and plot. Use [`fct_relevel()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/23_Data_transformation_advanced/Data_transformation_advanced.html#/change-order-of-levels-12) (Lesson 23) to turn the new variable into a factor with the categories in a meaningful order, from lowest to highest: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_06_cat <- wbns_06_cat |> mutate( ease_free_food_cat = fct_relevel( ease_free_food_cat, "Difficult access", "Moderate access", "Easy access" ) ) ``` ::: Spell each category exactly as you did in `case_when()`. If you get a warning about "unknown levels," a category name doesn't match. 4. **Check your categories.** Use [`tabyl()`](https://nwakim.github.io/PUBH_523_26F/lessons/28_Data_summarization_tables/Data_summarization_tables.html#/what-does-tabyl-do) to cross-tabulate the score with its new categorical version (Lesson 28): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_06_cat |> tabyl(ease_free_food, ease_free_food_cat) ``` ::: Each row (one score) should have counts in **only one** category column, and there should be **no** `NA_` column. An `NA_` column means some scores didn't fit into any of your ranges. 5. **Count people in each category** with `tabyl()` on just the new variable (e.g., `wbns_06_cat |> tabyl(ease_free_food_cat)`), and check that the categories print in the order you set. ::: {.panel-tabset group="project"} #### Project 1 Create **one** categorical variable: `ease_free_food_cat` from `ease_free_food` (possible range 4-20). Suggested categories, in order: | Scores | Category | |--------|----------| | 4-9 | "Difficult access" | | 10-15 | "Moderate access" | | 16-20 | "Easy access" | #### Project 2 Create **one** categorical variable: `trust_courtesy_respect_cat` from `trust_courtesy_respect` (possible range 2-10). Suggested categories, in order: | Scores | Category | |--------|----------| | 2-5 | "Low trust" | | 6-8 | "Moderate trust" | | 9-10 | "High trust" | #### Project 3 Create **two** categorical variables. You can create both in the same `mutate()`, separated by a comma. Lab 4 uses both. **`total_benefits_cat`** from `total_benefits` (possible range 0-9): | Number of benefits | Category | |--------|----------| | 0-1 | "0-1 benefits" | | 2-3 | "2-3 benefits" | | 4-5 | "4-5 benefits" | | 6-9 | "6+ benefits" | If very few people have 6 or more benefits, combine the last two into "4+ benefits" (4-9). **`mental_health_score_cat`** from `mental_health_score` (possible range 6-30). The suggested categories depend on the direction you chose when you built the score: | Option A (high = better) | Option B (high = worse) | Category | |--------|--------|----------| | 6-14 | 22-30 | "Frequent distress" | | 15-22 | 14-21 | "Some distress" | | 23-30 | 6-13 | "Little distress" | Either way, order the levels as `"Frequent distress"`, `"Some distress"`, `"Little distress"`. ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} #### Another way to make categories: `cut()` (optional) `cut()` is a function made specifically for turning a numeric variable into categories. It's not covered in our lessons, so `case_when()` is the main method in this lab, but you're welcome to use `cut()` instead. You'll also see it a lot in other people's code, so here's how it works. You give `cut()` the **break points** between categories and a **label** for each category: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wbns_06_cat <- wbns_05_composite |> mutate( ease_free_food_cat = cut( ease_free_food, breaks = c(3, 9, 15, 20), labels = c("Difficult access", "Moderate access", "Easy access") ) ) ``` ::: The tricky part is the break points. By default, each category **includes its upper break and excludes its lower break**. So `breaks = c(3, 9, 15, 20)` makes three ranges: more than 3 up to 9 (4-9), more than 9 up to 15 (10-15), and more than 15 up to 20 (16-20). That's why the first break is 3, not 4: a break of 4 would leave out a score of 4. This "off-by-one" mix-up is the most common mistake with `cut()`, so always check your categories with `tabyl()` the same way as step 4. Here are the break points that match the suggested categories: | Project | Score | `breaks` | |---------|-------|----------| | 1 | `ease_free_food` | `c(3, 9, 15, 20)` | | 2 | `trust_courtesy_respect` | `c(1, 5, 8, 10)` | | 3 | `mental_health_score` (Option A) | `c(5, 14, 22, 30)` | | 3 | `mental_health_score` (Option B) | `c(5, 13, 21, 30)` | | 3 | `total_benefits` | `c(-1, 1, 3, 5, 9)` | For `total_benefits`, the first break is -1 so that 0 is included. One nice thing about `cut()`: it returns a factor with the categories already in the order you listed them in `labels`, so you can usually skip step 3 (`fct_relevel()`). The `labels` always go from the lowest scores to the highest. The one exception is Project 3's mental health score with **Option B**: its labels are `c("Little distress", "Some distress", "Frequent distress")`, so you still need `fct_relevel()` to put "Frequent distress" first, like the other projects' order. ::: ::: callout-important #### Task Use `mutate()` with `case_when()` (or `cut()`) to create the categorical version(s) of your composite score(s), using the required name(s) from your project's tab.
